hints: Compare the starting material $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(Br)CH}_3$ with each product and decide whether Br has been replaced by another group or whether HBr has been removed to form a double bond.
For reaction 1, think about which source of $\text{OH}^-$ in water converts a C-Br bond into a C-OH bond.
For reaction 2, think about which nitrogen containing nucleophile replaces Br with an $\text{NH}_2$ group.
Recall why formation of an amine from a halogenoalkane needs a solvent that dissolves the nitrogen reagent and heating in a sealed apparatus.
For reaction 3, recall the specific solvent for $\text{OH}^-$ that favours removal of H and Br to form an alkene rather than substitution.
Check whether each reaction keeps the same carbon skeleton with a swap of groups or creates a C=C bond, then assign substitution or elimination.
walkthrough:
Read the skeleton change to sort substitution from elimination**
Look closely at the carbon skeleton. In reaction 1, $\text{Br}$ becomes $\text{OH}$ and in reaction 2, $\text{Br}$ becomes $\text{NH}_2$. The three carbons stay saturated, one group simply swaps for another, so both are substitution. In reaction 3, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(Br)CH}_3$ becomes $\text{H}_2\text{C=CHCH}_3$. You have lost HBr and gained a double bond, so that is elimination.

Choose the OH source for the alcohol**
To make $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ you need hydroxide ions as the nucleophile. Aqueous sodium hydroxide, $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, provides $\text{OH}^-$ in water and gives substitution to the secondary alcohol. Warming is usually used but aqueous condition is the key point.

Choose the nitrogen source for the amine**
To make $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CH}_3$ you need ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, as the nucleophile. Ammonia is dissolved in ethanol and the mixture is heated under pressure in a sealed tube. Ethanol dissolves both reagents and pressure prevents $\text{NH}_3$ escaping as a gas.

Switch the hydroxide solvent to force elimination**
The same $\text{OH}^-$ ion can act as a base instead of a nucleophile. When $\text{NaOH}$ is dissolved in ethanol and heated, it removes $\text{H}^+$ from a carbon next to C-Br while $\text{Br}^-$ leaves, forming propene. So remember the pattern: $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ favours substitution, $\text{NaOH}$ in ethanol with heat favours elimination.

Final answer: Reaction 1: $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, substitution.
Reaction 2: $\text{NH}_3$ in ethanol, heat under pressure, substitution.
Reaction 3: $\text{NaOH}$ in ethanol, heat, elimination.

hints: Focus on the only bond that is different in the two reactions, the $\text{C-X}$ bond that must break when $\text{OH}^-$ attacks.
Link the size of the iodine atom and the length and strength of the $\text{C-I}$ bond to the energy needed to reach the transition state.
walkthrough:
Identify the bond that controls the rate**
Both reactions break a carbon halogen bond to form the same alcohol. Iodine is larger than bromine with more inner shells and more shielding, so its outer electrons are further from the nucleus. The $\text{C-I}$ bond is therefore longer and weaker than $\text{C-Br}$.

Connect weaker bond to lower activation energy**
Breaking the $\text{C-X}$ bond is a key part of reaching the transition state. Because $\text{C-I}$ needs less energy to break, the activation energy $E_a$ for 2-iodopropane is lower. A lower $E_a$ means a larger fraction of molecules have enough energy at the same temperature, so the rate is faster.

Final answer: The $\text{C-I}$ bond is weaker than the $\text{C-Br}$ bond.
Less energy is needed to break $\text{C-I}$, so activation energy $E_a$ is lower and the reaction is faster.

hints: Start by deciding the polarity of the $\text{C-Br}$ bond from the electronegativities of C and Br, and remember that the bonding pair goes to the more electronegative atom.
Identify where the lone pair on $\text{CN}^-$ is located and which electron deficient carbon it attacks, then think about the direction of each curly arrow.
walkthrough:
Polarise the C-Br bond correctly**
Bromine is more electronegative than carbon, so the C-1 atom is electron deficient. Mark it $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and Br as $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. In substitution the $\text{C-Br}$ bonding pair leaves with Br. Draw a curly arrow starting on the $\text{C-Br}$ bond and pointing to Br, which becomes $\text{Br}^-$.

Attack with the carbon lone pair of cyanide**
The nucleophile is $^{-}\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$, with the lone pair and negative charge on carbon. Draw a lone pair on that carbon and a curly arrow from the lone pair to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of 1-bromopropane. This forms the new $\text{C-C}$ bond in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ while $\text{Br}^-$ leaves in one concerted SN2 step.

Final answer: Show $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ on C-1 of 1-bromopropane with curly arrow from $\text{C-Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}$ to form $\text{Br}^-$.
Show lone pair on C of $^{-}\text{CN}$ with curly arrow from lone pair to $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ (C-1) to form $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$.

hints: Remember that heating a nitrile with aqueous acid adds two molecules of water across the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ group to give a carboxylic acid plus an ammonium ion.
walkthrough:
Hydrolyse the nitrile to the acid**
The $\text{-CN}$ carbon becomes the $\text{-COOH}$ carbon, so butanenitrile gives butanoic acid. Under acidic conditions with $\text{HCl(aq)}$ and heat, you need $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and you produce $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$ alongside: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$$

hints: Track the change from $\text{-COOH}$ to $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ and count how many atoms of hydrogen from the reducing agent are needed to remove one oxygen as water.
walkthrough:
Balance the reduction with [H]**
Butanoic acid is reduced to butan-1-ol. The $\text{C=O}$ oxygen is removed as $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and two extra hydrogens are added to carbon. That is four atoms of hydrogen in total: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + 4\text{[H]} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Recall which powerful hydride reagent, used in dry ether, is required to reduce a carboxylic acid, since $\text{NaBH}_4$ is not strong enough.
walkthrough:
Select the strong enough hydride**
Carboxylic acids are very resistant to reduction. $\text{NaBH}_4$ will not do it. You need lithium tetrahydridoaluminate, $\text{LiAlH}_4$, in dry ether, which supplies hydride ions to reduce $\text{-COOH}$ all the way to $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$.
Final answer: $\text{LiAlH}_4$ (lithium tetrahydridoaluminate) in dry ether
